about: The one roadmap: phases, steps, dates and targets. ROADMAP.md and docs/index.html are generated from this file by python bench/bench_page.py. Status words: done (ran and checked), doing (being worked on), next, later. start/target/done are dates; a target is a proposal and may move, but the old one is kept in 'moved' when it does. measures are ids in coverage/measures.json.
goal: a mod or plugin author never launches Minecraft, and a modpack user need not diagnose mod conflicts by hand. Port source from any version to any other (and, separately, any loader to any other), resolve modpack incompatibilities, and prove behavior in the real game or a real server.

steps.title: F3Nope 1.21.5 → 1.21.6 on Fabric
steps.text: Port a real Fabric mod one minor forward: F3Nope 1.21.5 → 1.21.6, build + mixin audit.

steps.title: F3Nope backport 1.21.6 → 1.21.5
steps.text: Same mod backwards: untouched upstream 1.21.6 → 1.21.5, real client loads it.

steps.title: Prove behaviour, not just a build
steps.text: Prove a port's behaviour, not just its build. The first try (overlay inspected, AppleSkin inventory change 95.6%, save reloads at the same position) was re-marked to "loads" on 2026-10-26: a frame change and a save reload happen without the mod. Behaviour needs an assertion on the mod's own state (`--assert` on its class, `--expect-value` on its screen).
steps.result: `tools/tests/AppleSkinHudCheck.java` checks AppleSkin's HUD estimate against real regeneration on the 1.21.6 port, and fails when the estimate is broken on purpose.

steps.title: NeoForge end to end: Zombie Apocalypse 1.21.1 → 1.21.4
steps.text: Second loader end to end: NeoForge ZombieApocalypseAddon 1.21.1 → 1.21.4 with no hand edits; its `/za` command runs in a 1.21.4 world.

steps.title: Dependency blockers become one-file answers
steps.text: Dependency blockers become one-file answers: verified selection, disable with proof, and a reference that is not an `import` still counts (AppleSkin's JEI mixin).

steps.title: Refuse a port that still targets the old game
steps.text: A port refuses to pass while it still targets the old game: packaged metadata is read back.

steps.title: AppleSkin 1.20.1 → 1.21.6, five minors in one jump
steps.text: A five-minor jump on a bigger mod: AppleSkin 1.20.1 → 1.21.6. 62 errors down to 51 after seven rules (Identifier, food components, debug HUD); the rest needs real code changes.

steps.title: Render-pipeline changes become rules
steps.text: Turn the render-pipeline family into rules (draw texture / render pipeline / texture view), then re-run step 7 to a build.

steps.title: Build tools follow the target version
steps.text: Build-toolchain bumps follow the target automatically (AppleSkin needed Loom 1.10 + Gradle 8.13).

steps.title: 1.21.1 → 1.21.6 in one command, on two mods
steps.text: One command, no hand edits, for 1.21.1 → 1.21.6 on this mod, and the same for a second mod.

steps.title: Change index and version families
steps.text: Change index and hub-and-spoke families: every release from 1.14.4 to 26.3 diffed against the next in Mojang's names (`coverage/changes/`, `tools/ChangeIndex.java`), 24 families cut where an update breaks 1% or more of the game's names, each with a hub picked by Modrinth mod count, rule coverage and the best ledger run per step, shown in the porting map (`docs/index.html#porting`). Releases before 1.14.4 are listed as blocked (no official mappings).

steps.title: Hub router
steps.text: Router: `port` chains hops X → family hub → hub → … → Y from `coverage/changes/index.json`, one record per hop; renames inside a family applied from the index.
steps.result: `port --from A --to B --fix` walks the hubs, joins every update's renames and moves into one map by intermediary ids (`VersionMap --chain`), runs only the rules whose jump covers an update it crosses, builds once, and names the update behind each error left. Releases before 1.14.4 are refused. ZombieApocalypseAddon 1.21.1 → 1.21.4 (three families) builds and loads; → 1.21.6 stops at the same 9 errors as the one-jump path, all placed on 1.21.4 → 1.21.5; → 26.3 stops at 69 instead of 100+.

steps.title: Chain mappings across families
steps.text: Chain mappings across more than one family in a single port, with one record per hop.
steps.result: with 11b up to 1.21.11; updates into 26.x have no shared ids, so there the router relies on rules and names errors from the step files by name only.

steps.title: Rules learned from Stonecutter mods
steps.text: Learn rules from Stonecutter mods: 33 open-source multi-version mods pinned in `coverage/stonecutter/mods.json`, 5,045 `//? if` switches extracted with file, method and the update their boundary falls on (`bench/stonecutter_mine.py`). Changes made the same way in two or more mods became 38 rules in `knowledge/fixes.json` (22 forward, 16 backports), each with its switches as examples and a test that self-test re-runs (`bench/stonecutter_rules.py`).
steps.result: ZombieApocalypseAddon 1.21.1 → 26.3 stops at 50 errors instead of 69; → 1.21.6 (9) and the untouched Notes 1.21 → 1.21.6 (14) are unchanged, their errors have no repeated switch. The map shows rules learned per update.

steps.title: An untouched 1.20.1 mod to 1.21.6, loaded
steps.text: Prove one untouched mod from 1.20.1 (or older) to 1.21.6 to a build, then to a loaded client.

steps.title: Publish what each jump still needs
steps.text: Publish the family list each jump still needs, so a stop is a shopping list.

steps.title: Yarn to the game's own names, whole tree
steps.text: Convert a source tree from yarn to the game's own names (works for one version already; needs a full-tree pass).

steps.title: The build switches with the version (26.x)
steps.text: Switch the build with the version: Loom 1.17, Gradle 9.5, Java 25, no mappings.

steps.title: Name what moved in 26.3
steps.text: Diff the old official names against the 26.3 jar to name what moved.

steps.title: AppleSkin to 26.3, loaded in the client
steps.text: Port one mod to 26.3 to a build, then to a loaded client. AppleSkin NeoForge 1.21.6 → 26.3 reaches a packaged build with the mixin audit in 66s: build settings, NeoGradle, Java and 82 → 0 compile errors are handled by rules except the removed debug-text event, one hand-written file. Loading it in a real 26.3 client is the next rung.

steps.text: Fabric → NeoForge on one small mod, measured end to end.

steps.title: Forge → NeoForge and Fabric → Quilt
steps.text: Forge → NeoForge and Fabric → Quilt, which are close pairs.

steps.text: Publish which loader pairs are real, which are blocked, and why.

phases.title: Proof: behaviour in the real game and server
phases.intro: The second half of the goal, worked on alongside porting.

steps.title: Game checks on Linux and macOS
steps.text: Linux and macOS game checks (or label them), no-Java install on each.

steps.title: A mod's own behaviour asserted in a real client
steps.text: A mod's own behaviour asserted in a real client: AppleSkin's HUD estimate, Zombie Apocalypse Addon's zombies hunting with `/zhunt` on its 1.21.4 port; each fails when the mod is broken on purpose.

steps.title: Optional pixel comparison
steps.text: Optional pixel comparison for regressions, off by default.

steps.title: Paper plugins: plugin-check and server-check
steps.text: Paper plugins: `plugin-check` on MockBukkit (fast floor), then `server-check` on a real Paper server with a bot player following a scenario, secrets masked. AgentCraft passes, and each break made on purpose fails at its step.

steps.title: The bot joins any Paper version from 1.8
steps.text: The bot joins any Paper version from 1.8 through ViaProxy, reading each world's real floor and height.
steps.result: (1.8.8, 1.12.2, 1.16.5, 1.20.1 and 1.21.4 passed locally; CI covers 26.3 only)

steps.title: Nightly bot run on older Paper versions
steps.text: A nightly CI job runs the bot on older Paper versions.

steps.title: The bot joins a modded server
steps.text: The bot joins a modded server (NeoForge or Fabric dedicated server), so mods get scenario checks like plugins do.

steps.title: Port a Paper plugin between versions
steps.text: Port a Paper plugin between versions (SCOPE.md rung 5; config-only so far).

steps.title: Reproduce Sismeel's Forge 1.20.1 pack problems
steps.text: Reproduce Sismeel's Forge 1.20.1 pack problems: an item becomes a different block when placed, and a world fails to reopen. Identify the affected item and obtain or recreate the failing world; the supplied pack export has configurations and mod download references, but no world or logs. Determine each cause independently.
points: World that will not reopen: done. Traverse 7.0.12 bundles Biolith 1.0.1-alpha.1, which gives 7 Traverse biomes climate values of 3.01; Blueprint saves the overworld's biome list in full, and the next start rejects it ("Overworld settings missing"). Seen on the pack's real Forge server and in its real client (the save gets the datapack-failure screen). Biolith 1.0.1-beta.1 in mods/ fixes it: new worlds reopen, and a world saved by the broken version opens too.

Item that becomes another block: not reproduced. Every block item (14,129 in singleplayer), placed by a player's right-click on the pack's server and again in singleplayer with every client-only mod, land as themselves or as their own mod's deliberate variant (bamboo shoot, sapling stages, Craziness Awakened's random spawners); the 29 that change afterwards are vanilla rules (coral dying out of water) or the mod's own. No two mods override the same block look. 221 block names belong to blocks from two or more mods (e.g. "Azure Planks" in Outer End and Slugterra), the likeliest cause on the evidence; `pack-check` now lists them. Items are also placed on a wall, a ceiling and in water (ladders, hanging signs, spore blossoms, kelp). Sweet berries never place in this pack: Sizeable Foliage refuses it on purpose and plants its bush from "Sweet Berry Seeds" instead. The item's name from Sismeel is still needed.

steps.title: Detect and repair the failure, checked in the game
steps.text: Detect the demonstrated failure with a code check that fails on the broken case and passes on the corrected and normal cases; verify the correction and affected behavior in a real game, including save and reload when relevant. Preserve the original pack and world.
steps.result: `pack-check` saves every dimension the way level.dat stores it and reads it back, starts the same world a second time, and reads back every placed block; it fails on the shipped pack and passes with the repair. `PackCheckTest` covers the checks that need no game.

steps.title: Any installed pack or export as input
steps.text: Accept installed modpacks and exports as inputs, identify versions and loaders from evidence, and diagnose and repair proven incompatibilities with reversible changes and clear blockers. Expand across Minecraft versions and loaders with real pack cases.
steps.result: CurseForge exports and CurseForge app instances, both run in the game with `--fix` (a fixed .zip copy; an instance changed only after the recheck passes, and `--undo` restores it exactly). Jars no CurseForge list describes (other launchers' folders, hand-added jars) get their sides from Modrinth by SHA-1; a client-only mod neither site knows, and Forge does not name, still stops the game checks and is listed. Forge only in the game; repairs come from `knowledge/pack-fixes.json` (one entry).

steps.title: Random Things as a Forge port case
steps.text: Bring Random Things forward from its source as a Forge version-port case, and prove its behavior on the target version. Automatic Forge porting is not yet supported.
steps.result: its newest source is a partial 1.14.4 rewrite (36 files, 2019 MCP snapshot names); the full mod is 1.12.2.

phases.title: Testing without Minecraft open
phases.intro: Every check runs with no game window, and the cost of a game session is mostly shared, so many sessions run at once on one PC.

steps.title: Measure what one game session costs today
steps.text: Measure RAM, CPU, start time and time per check for one client, one dedicated server and one Paper server, warm and cold, as the baseline the next steps are judged against.
steps.result: bench/session_cost.py measures a session from the operating system on Windows, Linux and macOS. A hidden Fabric 26.3 client peaks at 1 GB and spends about 100 CPU-s starting, 49 with C1 only, which hidden launches now use; 16 started side by side from one saved launch. Warm on a hidden game: a screen check takes 3.9 s, a world check 3.0 s, a scripted scenario 5.1 s. mp-check's own dedicated server starts in 11 to 19 s. AgentCraft's scenario on a real Paper server takes about 51 s warm (130 CPU-s, 2.4 GB at the peak) and 316 s on a fresh clone, most of it Gradle reading and building the plugin for the first time. This PC is shared, so every point carries how busy it was.

steps.title: Every game check with no window
steps.text: ui-check, world-check, mp-check, eval and the behaviour checks run with no Minecraft window and no sound, with the same assertions and the same 1280x720 captures, and a check stops when a window asked to stay hidden is not.
steps.result: ui-check, world-check, eval and mp-check ran with the game hidden and quiet: no game window was on screen after any of 15 warm checks, nor at any half-second sample through a whole mp-check (its client and its own server), and each check kept its assertions and its 1280x720 framebuffer capture. The behaviour checks (AppleSkin's HUD estimate, Zombie Apocalypse's AI) ran hidden on a Linux machine with no screen at all. A check stops when a game asked to stay hidden reports its window library was not rewritten. The title screen no longer costs a fixed 4.5 s wait; it waits only while it fades in. The warm screen check (3.9 s) and scenario (5.1 s) are timed as the whole modaccel command; the 1.5 s and 2.9 s of October were the older Windows lane's own loop with a window, so they are not the same work.

steps.title: Check the game's data without launching it
steps.text: A check that needs the game's data but not its picture runs the game's own code with no window and no world: data-check reads what the mod registered, each item as a real stack, and every error the game logs while it loads the data packs. It costs about 5 CPU-s per check once one loaded JVM answers many checks, instead of 49 for a hidden client.
steps.result: modaccel data-check works on Fabric 26.3: on the Prism Lab demo mod it lists the mod's items, blocks, loot table and recipe with no game launched, and a broken recipe fails it with the game's own error. The game stays loaded: a changed data file costs about 2 CPU-s in 2 s, copied from src without Gradle when Gradle would copy it as it is. A spare game waits behind it, started up to just before the mods' own code, and takes changed code for about 5 CPU-s in 4 s; a changed mixin or loader file loads a fresh game, 12 s. The build is read once and kept until a build file changes. A loaded game holds about 0.38 GB.

steps.title: Many sessions at once on one PC
steps.text: modaccel runs at least 8 game checks side by side on this PC, each with its own game folder, without running out of memory; a hidden client starts on 25 CPU-s and a cold check takes under 10 s, and a waiting hidden client costs almost no CPU.
steps.result: 8 projects (copies of the demo mod) each ran data-check at once: from no game all passed within 26.6 s, about 21 CPU-s each and 4.5 GB at the peak; with their games loaded, all passed again within 6.3 s. The 8 loaded games hold 2.85 GB and their 8 spares 2.41 GB. A brand-new project's first check takes about 36 s, 21 of it Gradle reading the build and recording the launch. A hidden game nobody has asked anything for 2 s now draws 10 frames a second, woken at once by the next request: it uses 0.04 to 0.06 cores while waiting instead of 0.14 to 0.16, measured alternately on the same PC, with warm checks as fast as before. Tried and not used: Java's start-up cache for Paper (AOT) halves a start's CPU (48 to 24 CPU-s) but recording it adds about 95 s to one start and its shutdown, and the self-updating class archive saves 2 to 5 s per start but adds about 40 s to the first, a slow first start this step exists to avoid. Still to reach: a hidden client start of 25 CPU-s, a cold check under 10 s, and a server start of 10 s.

steps.title: Behaviour checks run nightly in CI
steps.text: The real-game behaviour checks (AppleSkin's HUD estimate, Zombie Apocalypse's AI) run every night in CI, not only on this PC.
steps.result: bench/behaviour_checks.sh runs both behaviour checks (AppleSkin's HUD estimate, Zombie Apocalypse's AI) in a hidden, quiet client on a virtual display with software OpenGL: on a fresh boat.dev Linux machine with no GPU both passed and both breaks failed, 10 minutes. The nightly CI job is written as bench/behaviour-nightly.patch with its expected spend ($0 on this public repository, about 10 to 15 runner-minutes a night) and waits for Jon to approve it.

steps.title: pack-check timed, and faster
steps.text: pack-check records how long each stage takes and checks the shipped and the repaired pack side by side.
steps.result: pack-check times every stage (read, static checks, each server start) and starts the repaired pack's server beside the shipped one. On Prehistoric World 2 (368 mods) a full check with the repair proven takes 5.1 minutes instead of 12.7, with the same findings. Client-only mods a start finds are remembered, so later runs skip that extra start; a start that only reads the world stops as soon as its probe is done; Simple Voice Chat gets a free port so the two servers do not collide, and a start that still loses a port runs again alone; a server that stops before its probe is done is reported at once instead of after the 20-minute timeout; an export is unpacked once. Tried for the 4.0-minute target and not used: the lighter compiler (C1) cuts a 368-mod server start's CPU by a third (519 to 351 CPU-s) but made the start take 465 s instead of 139 s; the item probe already uses 40 ms of every 50 ms server tick.

decisions.question: What is the goal?
decisions.choice: Any version to any version, any loader to any loader; today one hop inside one loader is verified

decisions.question: Can modpack users get compatibility help?
decisions.choice: Yes: diagnose and resolve installed-pack conflicts, with reversible changes and real behavior checks; `pack-check` covers Forge packs

decisions.question: Are version and loader changes the same job?
Does a passing build prove a port?
decisions.choice: No; loader-refused jars, invisible UI and unloaded mods all passed builds

decisions.question: What counts as progress?
decisions.choice: A row in `coverage/ledger.json` with a receipt, shown on the progress page

decisions.question: What do we support, and how does a new kind of project get in?
decisions.choice: `SCOPE.md`: platforms by side, a six-rung support ladder, intake through the `bench-new-mod` skill

decisions.question: Plugin ↔ mod conversion?
decisions.choice: Not for now; it's a rewrite, not a port, and hybrid servers already exist

decisions.question: Ports between Paper versions?
decisions.choice: Yes, as rung 5 for Paper once rungs 2–3 land

decisions.question: Where do roadmap steps, targets and every number we show live?
decisions.choice: `coverage/roadmap.json` (steps, dates, targets) and `coverage/measures.json` (every number, with its history and target); ROADMAP.md and the roadmap page are generated from them

decisions.question: How cheap should a game check be?
decisions.choice: 5 CPU-s per check, from 49. Checks that need the game's data but not a picture stop launching the game: data-check runs the game's own code with no window and no world (Jon, 2026-11-07, instead of sharing one started game). Picture checks keep the hidden client, with graphics settings as they are
